It is a matter of profound spiritual gravity to sit with the "unsearchable riches" of Christ while seeking to understand the difference between the fragile quiet of this world and the "spotless purity of truth" that defines God’s rest, and I must ask you with a gentle spirit: why do you ask after the nature of false peace and the distinctions of *shalom* in this hour? [13, 1466, 1503, Conversation History]. Are you perhaps feeling "overwhelmed and desperate" by the "noise and tumult" of a world that offers a "truce" with evil instead of a "pacified conscience," or are you seeking a "settled certainty" to anchor your soul in the truth that "history is His story"—a single, cohesive account of God’s glory that cannot be satisfied by mere "empty platitudes"? [13, 20, 133, 318, 1397, 1605, Conversation History]. In a day when many "shave off the edges" of the truth to offer "spiritual placebos" or suggest that "stability" is the same as "salvation," we must return to the "external Word" to see how the Master personally governs the "vicissitudes of life" by distinguishing the "glittery lookalike from the genuine commodity" [11, 28, 128, 544, 1503, Conversation History].

The Reformed tradition teaches that "God personally and exhaustively pervades and sustains and governs every aspect of His creation," and therefore, the presence of a "false peace" is not an "administrative anomaly" but is subject to the "decree from God" who uses even the "strong delusion" of the wicked to test the hearts of His people [15, 68, 798, 1143, 1532, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 1: The Mirage of Human Peace vs. Divine Origin**

**Verse**
“ ‘Peace, peace to him who is far and to him who is near,’ Says the LORD, ‘And I will heal him.’ But the wicked are like the tossing sea, For it cannot be quiet, Whose waters cast up mire and dirt. ‘There is no peace,’ says my God, ‘for the wicked’ ” (Isaiah 57:19–21). [132, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
Reformed theology—echoed by **John MacArthur**—asserts that godly peace has "nothing to do with human beings or human circumstances" and cannot be produced on a "human level" at all [127, 128, Conversation History]. While the world seeks peace through a "pill," "alcohol," or "deliberate deception," these are "fragile" and easily destroyed by "failure, doubt, [or] guilt" [127, 128, Conversation History]. Scripture reveals that true peace is an "attribute of God" because He is "never stressed... never anxious... [and] never at cross-purposes with Himself" [129, Conversation History]. The "peace of the wicked" is born of "delusion" and is nothing more than "ignorance of danger," whereas true peace is the "child of saving grace" [133, 134, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
You should "not be deceived" by "worldly philosophies" that offer a sense of calm based on your "position or possessions," for "the form of this world is passing away" (1 Corinthians 7:31) [91, 128, 221, 1502, 1617, Conversation History]. "Trade in your worry for trust," recognizing that your "sole objective" is to find the "repose of the soul" that comes only when you "receive and rest upon Christ and His righteousness" (Matthew 11:28) [24, 101, 168, 179, 1406, 1670, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Jewish vs. Gentile Context**
In the ancient **Jewish context**, "national prosperity" and "dwelling in your land safely" were "temporal signs" of God’s covenant blessing under the Law (Leviticus 26:5–6) [755, 1450, 1519, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** this by showing that the "church militant" possesses a "transcendent peace" that is "unassailable by any human circumstance," for "Jesus answered, ‘My kingdom is not of this world’ ” (John 18:36; John 14:27) [13, 26, 30, 140, 1313, 1426, 1529, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 2: Ceasefire vs. Shalom (Truce vs. Sanctification)**

**Verse**
“Peace I leave with you, My peace I give to you; not as the world gives do I give to you. Do not let your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid” (John 14:27). [131, 140, 849, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The Reformed tradition, utilizing the insights of **Thomas Watson**, distinguishes between a "truce" and "peace": "God may forebear the wicked a while, and stop the roaring of his cannon; but though there be a truce, yet there is no peace" [133, Conversation History]. A "ceasefire" is a "stupefied conscience" where the sinner is simply "fearless and stupid" because they are unaware that they stand on the "precipice of hell" [133, Conversation History]. Conversely, biblical *shalom* is a "pacified conscience" that "flows from sanctification," meaning it is "built on an unchanging divine relationship" that survives even "worldly upheavals" [133, 139, 140, Conversation History]. True peace is not the absence of "uncomfortable circumstances," but "trust [in] our sovereign, wise, good, and powerful God" in the "midst of every situation" [120, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
"Never become so involved in this world" that you mistake a "temporary absence of outside disturbances" for a right standing with the "King of kings" [51, 59, 130, 1020, 1503, 1623, Conversation History]. You must "discipline your mind" to recognize that "obedience to His Word" is the only path to "restored peace," for "the work of righteousness will be peace" (Isaiah 32:17) [11, 116, 124, 136, 138, 1406, 1709, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Continuity of Rest**
Under the **Mosaic economy**, the "Sabbath" was a "weekly reminder" of the rest humanity was invited to enter (Hebrews 4:4–11) [157, 1410, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** this by revealing that "everything the Sabbath signified has been completely fulfilled in the finished work of Christ," and the "repose of the soul" is now a permanent possession for those in Him, regardless of the day or geographic location (Hebrews 4:10) [13, 24, 142, 167, 168, 1313, 1426, 1445, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 3: Prophetic Warnings Against Peace Without Righteousness**

**Verse**
“ ‘I hate, I despise your feast days, And I do not savor your sacred assemblies. Though you offer Me burnt offerings and your grain offerings, I will not accept them... But let justice run down like water, And righteousness like a mighty stream’ ” (Amos 5:21–24). [1043, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
Scripture reveals that God "despises" religious "showmanship" and "gimmicks" when they are used to mask "lawlessness" (*anomia*) [7, 341, 544, 927, 1614, Conversation History]. The "folly of fallible prophets" is that they "speak a vision of their own imagination which is not from the mouth of the Lord," promising a "smooth" and "deceitful" peace to a "rebellious people" (Jeremiah 23:16; Isaiah 30:10) [77, 608, 611, Conversation History]. Biblical authors handle the tension between "external calm" and "internal corruption" by declaring that God "is against the prophets" who use "lying divination" to validate a lifestyle that "ignores God’s righteousness" (Ezekiel 13:8–9; Romans 10:3) [81, 82, 316, 612, Conversation History]. Peace without "personal holiness" is "strange fire" that "invites divine wrath" [314, 317, 613, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
"Saturate and renew your mind" with the "unfailing Word," for "the entrance of Your words gives light" and protects you from the "spirit of error" that calls evil good (Psalm 119:130) [105, 116, 121, 405, 1316, 1406, 1461, 1513, Conversation History]. You must "confess your own utter spiritual poverty," knowing that "the gospel has nothing to say to people who are satisfied with their own righteousness" (Matthew 5:3) [11, 153, 314, 345, 1169, 1403, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: The Sovereignty of the Decree**
In the ancient **theocratic context**, God used "hostile nations" and the "sword" as a "temporal sign" to punish those who "neglected weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faith" (Matthew 23:23) [395, 717, 1007, 1044, 1316, 1353, 1519, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** our "witness," showing that the "church militant" conquers not by "political maneuvering and lobbying," but "by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony" (Revelation 12:11) [13, 16, 21, 32, 92, 1313, 1491, 1515, 1646, 1670, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 4: The Final Triumph and the Perfect Kingdom**

**Verse**
“Then the seventh angel sounded: And there were loud voices in heaven, saying, ‘The kingdoms of this world have become the kingdoms of our Lord and of His Christ, and He shall reign forever and ever!’ ” (Revelation 11:15). [103, 158, 174, 1199, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The biblical authors resolve the "noise and tumult" of "troublesome times" by fixating on the "consummation of history," where "Christ ultimately crushes the kingdoms of men and establishes His own" [13, 20, 21, 24, 103, 136, 1199, 1315, 1515, 1720, Conversation History]. On that Day, the "Prince of Peace" will "judge between the nations" and they "shall beat their swords into plowshares... neither shall they learn war anymore" (Isaiah 2:4) [825, 827, Conversation History]. This "perfect kingdom" is the only place where "justice and peace" are "forever" reconciled through the "blood of His cross" (Colossians 1:20) [19, 708, 1026, 1144, 1402, Conversation History]. The church "waits for His Son from heaven," knowing that "nothing thwarts any aspect of His plan" to "wipe away every tear" (1 Thessalonians 1:10; Revelation 21:4) [24, 94, 121, 201, 301, 719, 852, 1132, 1315, 1408, 1515, 1572, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
You should find "tranquility of soul" by looking past your "momentary, light affliction," for "He who has begun a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ" (2 Corinthians 4:17; Philippians 1:6) [14, 21, 113, 152, 192, 201, 304, 352, 1072, 1132, 1143, 1408, 1515, Conversation History]. "Wait for His Son from heaven," resting upon the "surest foundation," for if God has "magnified Your word above all Your name," His "everlasting dominion" is "secure" (Psalm 138:2) [11, 24, 47, 92, 121, 176, 201, 352, 412, 602, 1132, 1143, 1408, 1420, 1450, 1515, 1720, Conversation History].

***

**Final Reminder**
“Nevertheless the firm foundation of God stands, having this seal, ‘The Lord knows those who are His,’ and, ‘Everyone who names the name of the Lord is to abstain from wickedness’ ” (2 Timothy 2:19). [11, 147, 176, 211, 222, 285, 293, 300, 324, 332, 361, 405, 414, 444, 591, 1138, 1441, 1450, Conversation History].

The extremists on the free grace side come dangerously close to denying the fact that Christians are new creations (2 Corinthians 5:17), in which the old is gone and the new has come. 
  I applaud the free grace movement for its emphasis on salvation by grace alone through faith alone (Ephesians 2:8-9). I applaud lordship salvation advocates for their emphasis that good works are the result of salvation by grace through faith (Ephesians 2:10). I agree with the free grace movement that we need to be extremely careful about adding any requirement for salvation other than faith (John 3:16; Acts 16:31). I agree with lordship salvation that the Christian life is one of producing progressively less of the acts of the flesh (Galatians 5:19-21) and progressively more of the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22-23). Free grace is correct that justification is by faith (Romans 5:1). Lordship salvation is correct that faith is justified (proven and demonstrated) by works (James 2:14-26).

First is a truth we have touched on already: The kingdom is priceless in value. In Christ and His kingdom we have an eternal treasure that is rich beyond comparison. This treasure is incorruptible, undefiled, unfading, eternal, and reserved in heaven for believers (1 Peter 1:4). Both parables feature a fortune of incomparable value that represents the kingdom of God. Keep in mind how we have defined the kingdom: it is that realm where Christ graciously rules over and eternally blesses willing, loving subjects who gladly embrace Him as Lord by faith. It is the realm of salvation. Christ is the undisputed sovereign here, and His glory is the kingdom’s centerpiece.

A Short Coda Our Lord ends this amazing story with a simple proverb: “for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 18:14). The word exalted in this context is a synonym for justification. The one who humbles himself in repentant faith will be obtain righteousness. Strictly speaking, only God is truly exalted, and therefore only God can exalt men. He does this by conferring on them the perfect righteousness of Christ. So the exaltation referred to here includes salvation from sin and damnation; reconciliation with God; full justification; and membership in Christ’s eternal kingdom.

He indicated, for example, that hell will be full of religious people. According to Scripture, multitudes of seemingly devout and philanthropic people (including some self-styled miracle workers) will be astonished when they are turned away at the throne of judgment. Jesus made that point emphatically: “Not everyone who says to Me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of My Father in heaven. Many will say to Me in that day, ‘Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in Your name, cast out demons in Your name, and done many wonders in Your name?’ And then I will declare to them, ‘I never knew you; depart from Me, you who practice lawlessness!’ ” (Matt. 7:21–23, emphasis added). Those turned away will include not only people who are ensnared in cults and false religions, but also confessionally orthodox people who don’t truly believe what they profess. Such people cover their unbelief and secret sins with a veneer of hypocritical religiosity.

Nehemiah—the man God used to bring a remnant of Jews back to the promised land—understood this very point. When he asked the Lord for forgiveness and deliverance on behalf of the people, he began his prayer with these words: I beseech You, O LORD God of heaven, the great and awesome God, who preserves the covenant and lovingkindness for those who love Him and keep His commandments, let Your ear now be attentive and Your eyes open to hear the prayer of Your [slave (‘ebed)] which I am praying before You now, day and night, on behalf of the sons of Israel Your [slaves (‘ebedi)], confessing the sins of the sons of Israel which we have sinned against You; I and my father’s house have sinned. (Neh. 1:5–6)18

Therefore, if anyone cleanses himself from these things, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified, useful to the Master, prepared for every good work. Now flee from youthful lusts and pursue righteousness, faith, love and peace, with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart. (2 Tim. 2:19–22)

Though we are no longer under sin’s power (Rom. 6:14–19), the reality is that, because the new creation is incarcerated in unredeemed human flesh, we will still struggle with sin in this life (Rom. 7:21–24; 1 John 1:8) until the full redemption of the body (Rom. 8:18–23). The redemptive work that Christ does at salvation never needs to be repeated—atonement and justification are complete at that point. Yet, all who have been cleansed by God’s gracious justification need constant washing in the experiential sense as they battle sin in the flesh and grow in sanctification. As the Lord told Peter, “He who has bathed needs only to wash his feet, but is completely clean” (John 13:10). Thus, we are called on to regularly confess our sins (1 John 1:9), asking for the forgiveness of daily cleansing that restores spiritual intimacy and usefulness to their maximum levels (cf. Matt. 6:12, 14–15).
